The dried-up salt lake of Uyuni is one of Bolivia's main attractions. It is the largest dried-up salt lake in the world, and its surface gleams and shimmers in the sunshine. In the rainy season, from November to March, the Uyuni Salt Flat becomes an enormous mirror: the honeycomb-shaped salt crust is covered by a very thin layer of clear water that reflects the sky. In the dry season, the lake's surface becomes a vast, flat, dazzlingly white desert. Its otherworldly beauty is remarkable throughout the year.

In the nearby village of Colchani, salt is still extracted using traditional methods. The healing properties attributed to the ancient hardened salt deposits have long been known locally. A hotel called Salt Hotel was built from blocks of salt, and stays there were believed to have a therapeutic effect on the respiratory systems of people suffering from bronchitis and other lung ailments.

A trip to Isla Pescado is particularly interesting for its distinctive ecosystem and the giant cactus growing there, described as the largest in the world. On the way to San Juan, a small and picturesque provincial town, a climb to the top of Ollagüe Volcano offers magnificent panoramas of the town and its surroundings; at Laguna Hedionda, you can admire flamingos. Visit the lagoons of Uyuni! From a scientific perspective, the Red Lagoon is a striking demonstration of ecosystem diversity. Its colour is attributed to algae and zoo- and phytoplankton containing trace metals. The saline water varies in colour from orange to violet, changing with the temperature. The lagoon reaches a depth of only 35 cm and is quite cold. By contrast, the geysers along the route are extremely hot and bubble vigorously. Eruptions of lava can reach 50 metres. The Polques hot springs offer a chance to refresh yourself in an oasis amid the desert. After lunch comes a visit to Licancabur Volcano and the Green Lagoon, whose emerald colour fully lives up to its name.

### Valdivia

Valdivia is a city with a rich history and many fascinating sights. One of Chile's principal seaports, it is situated 745 kilometres from Santiago and has a population of approximately 128,000. The city was founded on 9 February 1552 by the conquistador Pedro de Valdivia, the first governor of Chile. For many years, the settlement of Santa María la Blanca de Valdivia was one of the strongholds of the Spanish colonisers.

A number of remarkable historical landmarks have survived, especially the Spanish forts and fortifications. Valdivia has also been called the "city of rivers", the "pearl of the south", the "key to the southern seas" and the "Gibraltar of the Pacific", and is regarded as one of Chile's most beautiful cities.

Valdivia, Puerto Varas and Puerto Montt are relatively small cities located not far from one another. What brings them together is their setting in the Lake District. Beautiful lakes with thermal waters lie amid green landscapes. Here you can go water-skiing, kayaking and rafting.

## Leisure and activities in Valdivia

### Welcome to the city of four rivers!

Valdivia is one of Chile's most beautiful cities, drawing visitors with its scenic natural setting. The city lies on four rivers, making a river cruise an essential part of exploring it. Such an excursion offers views of the Botanical Garden, Teja Island and Austral University, as well as a visit to the fish market. Other highlights include the German-style beer restaurant La Cervecería Kunstmann, the sea lion colony on the waterfront, and the nearby towns of Niebla and Corral. Travelling in the second half of February also offers a chance to experience the famous Noche Valdiviana festival, a colourful celebration featuring decorated boats, fireworks and music.

Valladolid is a city made for walking and discovering what lies around the next corner. Low-rise houses retain colonial details, colourful walls alternate with wooden doors, and sunny streets lead to the main square. This Yucatán city turns a stop between Mérida and Cancún into a worthwhile part of the journey in its own right.

Begin in the centre at the Church of San Servacio, then follow Calzada de los Frailes towards the former Convent of San Bernardino de Siena in the Sisal neighbourhood. Along the way, take time to admire the façades and small courtyards. The Zací craft centre features embroidery and other work by local artisans. The San Roque Museum is a good place to learn about the city's history.

Yucatecan cuisine is another pleasure here. Try the local longaniza sausage for which Valladolid is known, and allow time for a leisurely lunch. Within the city is the Zací cenote, while Chichén Itzá and Ek Balam lie nearby. Valladolid is ideal for visitors who enjoy combining archaeology with everyday city walks and the flavours of local food.

The Valley of Rocks near Alota is included in a high-altitude journey through Bolivia. It is one of the natural stops along a route through the desert landscapes and lagoons of the country's southwest.

Exploring the rock formations complements a trip across the Uyuni Salt Flat. The details of the walk and the order of stops depend on the chosen itinerary.
